many-features.t: A table of six customers: each **column is one feature**, and each feature is one **dimension**. Here we show two real columns (usage and spend), but real tables can have **dozens or thousands**.

feature-space.t: Each customer becomes a **point on a plane**: usage frequency runs across and monthly spend runs up. Two features means two dimensions, so we can still see the whole dataset at once.

correlated-features.t: The points climb from lower left to upper right, and the dashed line follows them. Customers who **visit more also spend more**: the correlation is **0.94**.

redundancy.t: Two columns, but largely **one story: how engaged the customer is**. The short dashed lines show how little each point departs from the trend, so the second column adds little that is new.

three-d-view.t: Adding a third feature, such as sessions, that also tracks engagement keeps the points close to **one line through 3-D space**. This is an illustration, not real data. More columns do not always mean more information.

hard-to-visualize.t: With **40 features** there would be 40 axes. We cannot draw them, and distances between points become less informative. This is a main reason to reduce dimensions.

compress.t: Each point drops onto the trend line. Its **position along the line** is what we keep, and its small **distance from the line** is the detail we give up.

one-d-view.t: Laid out on a number line, each customer is now a single number: its position along the trend. **Six numbers replace twelve.**

preserve-structure.t: We kept the **order and spacing along the trend** and lost only the small departures from it. **Remember:** dimensionality reduction trades a little detail for a much simpler description.
